stemBlocks.value: Rewrite y = x² + 4x − 5 in completed-square form and hence state the coordinates of its turning point.
Think first: Completed-square form hands you the turning point directly — no differentiation or table of values needed.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p102-q12 from workbook page 102.

solutionSteps.instruction: Halve the coefficient of x and square it.

contentBlocks.value: half of 4 is 2, and 2² = 4, so x² + 4x = (x + 2)² − 4

solutionSteps.instruction: Substitute back and combine the constants.
Find the x-value that makes the square zero.
Read off the corresponding y-value, which is the constant term.

strategyBlocks.value: Write y as (x + h)² + k, then read the turning point off as (−h, k).

finalAnswerBlocks.value: y = (x + 2)² − 9; the turning point is (−2, −9), and it is a minimum.

whyThisWorks.value: In the form y = (x + h)² + k the graph is the basic parabola y = x² shifted h units horizontally and k units vertically. The vertex of y = x² sits at the origin, so after the shift it sits at (−h, k). Because the x² coefficient is positive, that vertex is the lowest point of the curve.

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the turning point as (2, −9) — the x-coordinate is the value that makes the bracket zero, so the sign flips.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Giving the turning point as (2, −9) — the x-coordinate is the value that makes the bracket zero, so the sign flips.

examTip.value: For y = a(x + h)² + k the turning point is always (−h, k) — memorise the sign flip and state whether it is a maximum or a minimum.
